items.title: NeperOS Dynamic: apps from a prompt, compiled in Neper on a server, scanned, installed
items.evidence: Queued by the user (2026-10-08). Dynamic is the app that makes apps: the user writes a prompt that says what app they need; the prompt goes to a NeperOS server that has a model write the app in the Neper language, compiles it, security scans it, and sends the result back to be installed on the device; no compiler, editor, IDE, debugger or linter on the phone; a Dynamic app can be extended later with extra features by another prompt. Acceptance: (1) the prompt screen (a text field on the on-screen keyboard, the apps already made, a progress view with the stages: written, compiled, scanned, ready), and the follow-up prompt on an existing app that sends its source and the request and gets a new version; (2) the server side as a documented protocol over C117's TLS: a request carries the prompt, the app's identity and the device's API level; the answer carries the app image, its source, its manifest (name, icon, the capabilities it asks for) and a signature; the source stays on the server and on the device for extension; (3) the compile step is the Neper compiler against the NeperOS app kit (appkit, text, scenes, the e.* library) with the diagnostics fed back to the model for repair until it builds or gives up with a readable message; (4) the security scan: the manifest's capabilities are checked against what the code calls (no raw syscall or MMIO outside the app kit; no network unless declared; no storage outside the app's own directory), the build is reproducible, the image is signed by the server, and the device verifies the signature and the manifest before installing; the first run shows the capabilities and asks; (5) install: the image lands under the app's own directory, the icon joins the home grid, an app can be removed, updated and rolled back; the kernel launches it with only the capabilities granted; (6) limits and honesty: a Dynamic app is generated code, labelled so; resource limits and a kill switch; the server keeps an audit log and can revoke a signature; (7) a fixture against a local test server with a canned model answer (no live model in the suite) that goes prompt to installed icon to launch to extension. Not queued here: sharing apps between users, a store, paid generation, on-device compilation.

items.title: NeperOS stage 2: the kernel as an AVF guest on a Pixel (crosvm bring-up)
items.evidence: Opened by D2143 when C103 closed D2119 stage 1. Acceptance (D2119 stage 2): the same microkernel boots as an Android Virtualization Framework guest that crosvm starts with the Linux arm64 boot protocol -- device tree in x0, GICv3, PSCI 1.0, an ns16550 serial console, and virtio console, block and vsock over PCI -- first under crosvm, then on a retail Pixel via `adb shell vm run` as a non-protected VM. Device addresses are read from the device tree, never hard-coded; the virtio-pci transport already serves both. Done (D2144): the ns16550/8250 console -- neperos/src/ns16550.e drives the 8250 (THR at 0, LSR at 5 bit 5), the kernel picks it vs PL011 from the stdout uart node's `compatible` (ns16550a for crosvm, arm,pl011 for virt), base and reg-shift from the device tree; console_write and the console server's device_write dispatch by a boot-set flag. Written to crosvm's actual source (aarch64/src/fdt.rs: compatible ns16550a, reg=<addr size>, no reg-shift => shift 0) and regression-verified under QEMU virt (the tree selects PL011, all stage-1 marks pass, ns16550 path inert). Also extracted crosvm's aarch64 memory map from source (RAM 0x80000000, GIC/PCI bases). BLOCKER confirmed (D2144): crosvm is built and runs in this WSL but is KVM-only with no CPU emulation, and the host is x86-64, so it cannot run the aarch64 kernel (rejected as a bad bzImage). Verifying the crosvm/AVF boot -- and the remaining pieces, a virtio-vsock driver and the crosvm memory-map boot -- needs an aarch64 host (a Pixel via adb, or an aarch64 Linux box with KVM); surfaced to the user as a resource decision. Advanced (D2145): the EL0 user window moved to the top of the 39-bit space (index 511, VA 0x7FC0000000) so it no longer collides with crosvm's RAM at 0x80000000, which would otherwise have unmapped the kernel from every user space on the first trap; QEMU-verified -- kernel boots, every EL0 server runs, isolation holds (thread W faults at 0x7FC0040000, X at kernel RAM 0x40000000, Q at ECAM 0x4010000000). The chosen aarch64 host is an AWS Graviton bare-metal instance (only *.metal exposes /dev/kvm for crosvm's KVM backend); the account's configured AWS credentials are invalid and await refresh. The kernel image already carries a valid arm64 Image header. VERIFIED ON REAL HARDWARE (D2146, AWS a1.metal Graviton bare-metal with /dev/kvm): the kernel boots under crosvm/KVM, reads crosvm's DTB (RAM 0x80000000, GICv3, ns16550 at 0x3f8), turns the MMU on and runs the whole EL0/capability suite -- D2145 confirmed, thread W faults at the relocated window 0x7FC0040000. Two crosvm-vs-QEMU gaps found and fixed: crosvm's PCI host is CAM (pci-host-cam-generic, shifts bus<<16/slot<<11/fn<<8) not ECAM, now detected by compatible with a cam flag in pci.Host; and a virtio device's BAR is the one its capabilities name (BAR0 on crosvm, pre-assigned; BAR4 on QEMU, guest-assigned), now discovered and mapped at its real size instead of a hard-coded BAR4/64KB. All three drivers then run under crosvm: entropy returns 8 bytes, block reads/writes sector 0, console writes a virtio-console port; QEMU's ECAM path unchanged (stage-1 boot still green). D2147 then closed the last crosvm functional gap: the EL0 page mappings were global (missing the nG bit), so on a real Cortex-A72 (not QEMU's interpreter) a thread's USER_BASE TLB entry served another thread after the ASID-only context switch, making the console-server client read a neighbour's 0xCD poison and a round-printer re-run. Marking the EL0 leaf descriptors non-global fixed it; the WHOLE stage-2 demo now runs clean under crosvm/KVM on AWS a1.metal -- all three virtio drivers, the capability/isolation threads, `console server up` over the P->K server, `all threads done` and a PSCI power-off with exit 0 -- and QEMU's stage-1 boot is byte-unchanged. D2149 added the virtio-vsock driver (EL0 server T): vsock_connect sets up the three queues (rx/tx/event), reads the guest CID from device config (passed via a new aux slot 5), transmits a STREAM REQUEST to host CID 2, and reads the reply. Verified on AWS a1.metal under crosvm `--vsock cid=3` over /dev/vhost-vsock -- no listener gave op 3 (RST), a Python AF_VSOCK listener on port 1234 gave op 2 (RESPONSE) with the host logging the accept from (3, 1024), a full round trip. QEMU has no vsock device so T is skipped and stage 1 is unchanged. The whole crosvm device list (console, block, vsock over PCI) is now done. Remaining before score 1: the same kernel on a retail Pixel via `adb shell vm run`. NeperOS stages 3 (bare-metal Pixel 6) and 4 follow (D2119).

items.title: NeperOS shell 3: the e.os surface on NeperOS (os.neperos.e)
items.evidence: Queued by D2148. Acceptance: an `os` variant for target `aarch64 neperos` over NeperOS system calls -- memory from untyped/frame capabilities, threads, monotonic time from the counter and wall time from the RTC the device tree names (PL031 on virt), file I/O through the C106 server, stdout and stderr through the console server; e.io, e.fs, e.time, e.thread and e.fmt compile unchanged for NeperOS, and their existing fixtures that need no network pass under QEMU. BEGUN D2154 (lib/e/os.neperos.e): the e.os surface is intrinsic-based (compiler seeds open/read/write/close/seek/stdout/stderr/exit/threads/clock into e.os; the per-target variant file adds helpers), and NeperOS had no variant -- it fell back to the types-only os.e. New os.neperos.e is the variant project.select_source picks for a neperos os (a variant is the whole module: full type block + ErrorKind/ErrorDetail + NATIVE_SEPARATOR + read_detail/write_detail over the seeded read/write). e.io now compiles and RUNS unchanged on NeperOS, verified on QEMU both hosts: io_test.e reaches os.stdout() + a Writer via io.print (not the console primitive), prints two lines, exit 0; fixtures in run.ps1/run.sh. Existing neperos programs (init, shell/fs servers) unaffected (seeded intrinsics + base types only). e.time DONE (D2155): os.clock lowered to kernel syscall 13 -- monotonic from the virtual counter converted to ns, wall from the PL031 RTC the device tree names, verified on QEMU both hosts (time_test.e: elapsed ns across a spin + a 2026 wall timestamp). e.fmt DONE (D2156): the 45 fmt codecs are pure (no os primitive), so the variant + e.io carry them -- fmt_test.e encodes a struct with json.encode[T] to an e.io Writer, verified both hosts. e.thread DONE (D2157): os.thread_create spawns a thread in the same address space on a kernel-mapped stack (vm.map_stack in the spare L3 entries above the program window), join reuses the reap syscall, detach is syscall 15; a by-pointer Thread arg caused a non-blocking-join race (99 on Windows QEMU, 0 on Linux) until the wrapper dereferenced it, now 5/5 on each host. e.fs DONE (D2158): file I/O through the C106 server -- un-seed open/read/write/close/seek/readdir for neperos, add a console_write intrinsic for stdout, and write the file surface in os.neperos.e as a client-side handle model over fsproto IPC (open/read/write/close/stat/mkdir/remove real, symlink/rename/dirs/env Unsupported); fs_efs.e writes+reads /hello through the server, both hosts. ALL FIVE MODULES (e.io/e.time/e.fmt/e.thread/e.fs) now compile+run on NeperOS. Last 0.1 (thread_create/join/detach), e.fs (the ~40 path/dir/stat functions over the C106 server), e.fmt breadth, and porting the existing lib fixtures to run under QEMU. Last 0.1: stdout through the EL0 console server (now the kernel console write); the Unsupported fs ops the flat C106 server cannot serve; and porting the lib modules' own existing fixtures to NeperOS beyond the one-per-module here. D2183: e.fmt BREADTH -- fmt_test.e now also writes two rows through e.fmt.csv (a header and a data row, the default comma/LF dialect) after the json encode, so the serial reads `fmt csv: x,y,label` then `3,7,neperos`; a second pure e.fmt codec runs unchanged on NeperOS, identical on both QEMU hosts (8.2 WSL, 11.1 Windows). Built and verified with a worktree-local neper-self (~17s via the Windows bootstrap) because the shared one had been swapped by a concurrent session to a divergent line lacking this worktree's D2158 write-seed guard (resolve.e:436 keeps open/read/write/close/seek out of the seeded intrinsics for neperos so the variant defines them). D2184: a THIRD codec -- fmt_test.e also encodes the struct through e.fmt.ini (flat key=value: `x=3`/`y=7`/`label=neperos`), so three pure e.fmt codecs (json/csv/ini) run unchanged on NeperOS, identical on both QEMU hosts. Boundary found: only the SHELL boot is verifiable here; the gpu/DRIVER boot faults at the program's first instruction (unexpected exception 0x08, far 0x10000000000, exit 0x87) for every driver program incl. the unmodified, previously-green gpu_test/calc_app/clock_app -- the same binaries run under the shell boot. Two independent compilers (c103b self-host rebuilt today + build/windows/neper.exe), both from the divergent C103/master line that overwrote the shared build/, produce the IDENTICAL fault; no fa07c7d0-line compiler is available and one cannot be built here (frozen bootstrap lacks capacity, WSL crashes on the self-host build, Windows bootstrap needs absent MSVC). So the gpu-boot C107 fixtures and the C112-C114 app-face rendering are unverifiable until the branch lands on master / a matching toolchain is restored -- a coordination state, not a code defect. D2185: e.thread GROUP -- thread_test.e now also runs thread.spawn_all/join_all (three workers over three contexts, one barrier; each write checked after join_all), serial `thread group of 3 joined`, both QEMU hosts. This also sharpens the boundary: the toolchain miscompile is NARROW -- thread_test drives os.thread_create + vm.map_stack (page-table code of the same family as the faulting map_range_el0) and runs correctly on the shell boot with the same neper-self that faults the driver boot, so only the device-MMIO driver-boot path is affected; the rest of the e.os surface (e.io/e.time/e.fmt/e.thread spawn+join+group) stays verifiable. D2186: e.time CALENDAR breadth -- time_test.e now converts the wall timestamp to a civil date via time.to_date (days_from_civil/civil_from_days floor-division math) and prints `time date 2026-10-7`, proving the calendar path runs on NeperOS beyond the raw clock read; fixtures assert a `time date 20xx-` pattern, both QEMU hosts. Confirmed the C113/C114 faces render via e.gpu's CPU backend (no real GPU) but need the 16MB out-of-window arena, which both the driver boot and start_process's bigarena path get through the one miscompiled map_range_el0 (main.e:85), and the 2MB in-window cap is far too small -- so the faces are sound but verifiable only with a matching toolchain. D2187: e.io BUFFER round-trip -- io_test.e now, after the two stdout prints, writes seven bytes through an io.SliceWriter and reads them back through an io.SliceReader over the written portion (bytes and both counts checked), serial `io roundtrip ok`, both QEMU hosts. The verifiable e.os surface now has shell-boot breadth across all four shell-reachable modules: e.io (stdout + buffer round-trip), e.time (clocks + civil date), e.fmt (json/csv/ini), e.thread (spawn+join+group). C107 holds at its ~0.9 ceiling here: e.fs's remaining ops are flat-C106 Unsupported-by-design and its driver-boot fixtures (plus the C112-C114 rendering) need a matching toolchain, so further shell-boot breadth adds coverage without moving the score.

items.evidence: `e.gpu` at `surface: partial`: `open`/`close`/`has`/`info`, `queue` and `queue_with`, `Buf[T]` as a generation-checked handle into a per-device table, `alloc`/`upload`/`write`/`download`/`release`/`len`, tokens with `done`/`wait`/`wait_for`, `sync`, `grid1/2/3`, and `gpu.launch[K]` as the third argument-pack intrinsic: the pack is checked against the kernel's parameters (`Buf[T]` for a device slice, a value of the parameter's type otherwise) and expands into a generated launcher per calling module, kernel and argument shape (D778). `gpu.barrier()` is the third device intrinsic recognised, legal only in a kernel's own body, lowered as the cut of the CPU build (D780). The fault buffer (D785): a failed tag, alignment, null, enum or bounds check in a kernel's CPU build writes the queue's one `FaultRecord` and ends the invocation, `sync`/`download` answer `Fault` once, `last_fault` answers the record. The device block now has a reentrant mutex covering queue, buffer and close operations; a short registry lock protects publication and token lookup, and CPU launches serialize their shared scheduler globals (D1788). `link/gpu_device_lock` passed ten Windows runs on CPU and both Vulkan devices, and passed Linux's CPU/no-device path. Existing GPU staging, sync, CPU, gaps and presentation fixtures pass on Windows; staging passes Linux's CPU/no-device path. Not yet: full-suite verification. items.title: Work-stealing pool, parallel parse and codegen
items.evidence: the front end runs in waves of eight workers (D321); the modules are lowered, selected and written as artifacts on eight workers with checkers that share the declarations (D325); and the same workers check the bodies and build both inlining oracles first, each with a checker forked from the program's and importing the types of a body copied from another worker's oracle (D326). A two-million-line program builds cold in 7.6 s debug and 7.4 s release where it took 29 and 26, its body sweep 0.6 s where it took 1.9 (1.3 s where it took 5.7 in release), the settle nothing on a cold build and the lowering not re-checking what the sweep checked (D327), and the bootstrap runs a thread inline. The names are validated on the workers too (D328), the artifact writer copies bytes with one runtime call (D329), and the allocator, the digest and the lexer lost their last quadratic and per-byte costs (D330): a million-line program builds cold in 3.0 s on Windows and 3.4 s on Linux, warm in half a second; the link's per-artifact passes run on the workers too, with SHA-256 and CRC-32C in hardware where the CPU has them (D336): a million-line program builds warm in a quarter of a second, the compiler in 65 ms; what remains sequential is collecting the declarations, reachability and layout; the work is assigned statically, not stolen Stealing modules through a shared counter was built and measured, and reverted (D1578): the compiler's body phase is bound by its largest module (`check.e`), which no worker can split, and on sc500k the lowering lost the static schedule's balance (1.7-1.9 s against 1.3-1.5 s); the lever left is stealing a module's functions, across the D326/D327 coupling of checks to lowering. Moved to the end of the queue by the user's decision (D1579): what is left needs the declaration tables redesigned -- per-module tables merged in module order with every index relocated -- for at most the 152 ms of a 2.16 s sc500k build the declarations take (resolve 74 ms, the link from artifacts 130 ms), or function-level stealing across the D326/D327 coupling.

items.title: AES-GCM at OpenSSL's speed: AES and carry-less multiply instructions for e.crypto.aead
items.evidence: e.crypto.aead's AES-GCM is portable Neper, a bitsliced AES (BearSSL's aes_ct64) and a GHASH from masked integer products (ghash_ctmul64), D1645. Measured 2026-09-28 on the Core i5-12500H, sealing one TLS record: 11.6 us for 100 bytes and 702 us for 16 KB (23 MB/s), against OpenSSL's 0.73 us and 3.19 us (5.1 GB/s, through Python's cryptography 48, whose call overhead is included): 16 times slower on small records and 220 times on large ones. It bounds every TLS user: x.microsoft.tds scans SQL Server at 28-35% of the fastest language (D1643), where OpenSSL, Go and rustls run AES-NI and PCLMULQDQ. Closing the gap needs the back end to emit AESENC/AESENCLAST and PCLMULQDQ (x64) behind a CPU check with the portable path as the fallback, as SHA-256 and CRC-32C already are in the link (D336), then a GCM that keeps its expanded key and H powers across records (e.net.tls expands the key for every record today) and runs four to eight blocks in flight. Until then, the portable path's own lever is codegen: the same bitsliced rounds run at about 130 cycles a byte, several times BearSSL's in C.

items.title: Fast, small PNG encoding: dynamic Huffman, lazy matching and table CRC
items.evidence: Backlog from the chart benchmark (D2108, D2110). On the same 360x240 chart raster, e.fmt.png at .Balanced takes about 18 ms and writes 14,004 B, while zlib level 6 with the same filter-0 rows takes 1.74 ms for 11,283 B; rasterizing takes 2.0 ms, so the encoder is the whole PNG gap to matplotlib. e.algo.deflate writes fixed-Huffman blocks only (zlib restricted to fixed Huffman gives 12,903 B, so dynamic trees are worth about 1.6 KB here), has no lazy matching and restarts its 16-deep hash chain at every 32 KiB block (about 1.1 KB more), and e.fmt.png computes CRC-32 bit by bit. Done when: e.algo.deflate writes dynamic-Huffman blocks with lazy matching and a window that spans blocks, round-tripping through its own decoder and Python's zlib on a corpus; e.fmt.png uses a table-driven CRC; the chart benchmark's PNG pass is at least as fast as matplotlib's with files no larger than zlib level 6 on the same rows; both suites pass. Adaptive per-row filters are optional: Pillow's heuristic made this chart larger.
